title: Nunavut
wiki_lead:
Nunavut is the largest and northernmost territory of Canada. It was separated from the Northwest Territories in 1999, via the Nunavut Act and the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act, which provided this territory to the Inuit for self-government. The boundaries were drawn in 1993. The creation of Nunavut resulted in the first major change to Canada's political map in half a century since the province of Newfoundland, known as Newfoundland and Labrador since 2001, was admitted in 1949.
Nunavut comprises a major portion of Northern Canada and most of the Arctic Archipelago. Its vast territory makes it the fifth-largest country subdivision in the world. Nunavut's capital and Canada's smallest capital by population, Iqaluit, formerly "Frobisher Bay", on Baffin Island in the east, was chosen by the 1995 Nunavut capital plebiscite. Other major communities include the regional centres of Rankin Inlet and Cambridge Bay.
Nunavut includes Ellesmere Island in the far north, the eastern and southern portions of Victoria Island in the west, and all islands in Hudson Bay, James Bay and Ungava Bay, including the western portion of Killiniq Island in the southeast and Akimiski Island far to the south of the rest of the territory. Nunavut is Canada's only geopolitical region that is not connected to the rest of North America via the Pan-American Highway.
Nunavut is the least densely populated major country sub-division in the world, not considering Antarctica, being even less densely populated than Greenland. With a population of 36,858 as of the 2021 Canadian census, up from 35,944 in 2016, consisting mostly of Inuit, and a land mass almost as large as Mexico, Nunavut's land area of 1,836,993.78 km2 (709,267.26 sq mi) has a population density of 0.022/km2 (0.056/sq mi).
Alert, Nunavut, is the world's northernmost continuously inhabited place. Eureka, a weather station on Ellesmere Island, has the lowest average annual temperature of any Canadian weather station.

History


Early history
The region which is now mainland Nunavut was first populated approximately 4,500 years ago by the Pre-Dorset, a diverse Paleo-Eskimo culture that migrated eastward from the Bering Strait region.
The Pre-Dorset culture was succeeded by the Dorset culture about 2,800 years ago. Anthropologists and historians believe that the Dorset culture developed from the Pre-Dorset.
Helluland, which Norse explorers described visiting in their Sagas of Icelanders, has been associated with Nunavut's Baffin Island. Claims of contact between the Dorset and Norse are controversial.
The Thule people, ancestors of the modern Inuit, began migrating from Alaska in the 11th century into the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. By 1300, the geographic extent of Thule settlement included most of modern Nunavut.
The migration of the Thule people coincides with the decline of the Dorset. Thule people genetically and culturally completely replaced Dorset some time after 1300.

grok_lead: Nunavut is the northernmost, largest, and newest territory of Canada, formed on April 1, 1999, by partitioning the eastern Northwest Territories to establish public government for the predominantly Inuit population under the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement, the largest Aboriginal land claim settlement in Canadian history. Spanning roughly 2,000,000 square kilometresâone-fifth of Canada's landmassâit encompasses Arctic tundra, islands, and freshwater, with extreme climatic conditions including polar nights and days, permafrost, and minimal tree cover. The capital and largest community is Iqaluit on Baffin Island, serving as the seat of the territorial legislature. The territory's population stands at approximately 36,000, with Inuit people constituting about 85 percent, underscoring its role as a homeland for Inuit self-determination amid vast geographic isolation accessible primarily by air or sea. Governed through a consensus-based Legislative Assembly without political parties, Nunavut exercises devolved authority over resources and lands but depends heavily on federal transfers, reflecting ongoing negotiations for fuller control. The economy centers on public administration, mining (notably diamonds and gold), commercial fisheries, and subsistence harvesting integral to Inuit cultural continuity, though challenged by high costs, skill gaps, and environmental constraints. Nunavut's creation marked a milestone in Indigenous land rights and northern governance, enabling Inuit-led policies on education, language (Inuktut as co-official), and wildlife management, yet it grapples with socioeconomic disparities including elevated rates of poverty, food insecurity, and youth suicide linked to rapid modernization and colonial legacies. Resource development promises growth but sparks debates over ecological impacts in a fragile Arctic ecosystem increasingly affected by climate change.
